claims.claim: A drainage basin (also called a watershed or catchment) is the area of land from which water flows to a common stream or outlet, and ridges or hills that separate two watersheds are the drainage divide.

Discharge is the volume of water moving down a stream or river per unit of time, commonly expressed in cubic feet per second or gallons per day, and is computed by multiplying the channel cross-sectional area by the average velocity of the water.

Stream gradient is determined by dividing the change in elevation between two points by the distance between them, and water flow in a stream is primarily related to gradient while also being controlled by channel geometry.

A stream transports material as bedload (large particles moved by rolling, sliding, or saltation, often only during high flows), suspended load, and a dissolved load that on average makes up about 15 percent of the mass of material transported.
The faster water flows, the larger the particles that can be kept in motion, and when velocity drops the stream deposits material, with coarser grains settling first.

When a river overtops its banks during floods, the coarsest sediment is deposited near the channel edge, building low ridges called natural levees, while progressively finer sediment is deposited across the floodplain beyond.

In a meandering channel the stream erodes the banks on the outside of a curve and deposits on the inside, forming a point bar, and over time the sinuosity becomes increasingly exaggerated as the channel migrates within its flood plain.
Where a stream enters a still body of water, such as a lake or the ocean, sediment is deposited and a delta forms; the Fraser River has created a large delta extending into the Strait of Georgia.

An alluvial fan is a fan-shaped deposit of sand and gravel formed where a stream emerges from a mountainous area onto flatter ground, because the sudden decrease in gradient slows the water and causes deposition of its load.

Base level is the lowest level a stream can erode down to, and a graded stream erodes its drainage basin into a smooth profile that is steepest in its headwaters with a gradient that decreases gradually downstream, transporting its load without major net erosion or deposition.

Flooding is natural river behavior: discharge levels vary with the time of year and the weather, flood frequency is described by recurrence intervals, and a 100-year flood is a flood with a 1-percent annual exceedance probability rather than a flood that occurs once per century.

The water cycle moves water among the atmosphere, land, and ocean through evaporation, evapotranspiration, condensation, precipitation, snowmelt, runoff, streamflow, infiltration, and groundwater recharge; rivers are the streamflow branch returning land water toward the ocean.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The '100-year flood' label is widely misunderstood as a fixed schedule.
positions: USGS Water Science School: a 100-year flood is a flood with a 1-percent annual exceedance probability; the term describes a flood of great magnitude and is often misinterpreted as a once-per-century event.
Open Textbook BC: flood frequency is quantified with a recurrence interval computed as Ri = (n+1)/r from the record of annual peak discharges.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson explains the 1-percent annual probability meaning explicitly and states that such floods can occur twice in a decade or not at all for centuries; it avoids any claim that these floods arrive on a fixed schedule.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The simple rule that faster water moves larger grains glosses over fine-particle behavior.
positions: USGS Water Science School: fast-moving water can pick up, suspend, and move larger particles more easily than slow-moving water.

Open Textbook BC (Hjulstrom-Sundborg diagram, flagged in the sibling erosion topic's research): silt and clay grains cohere and require higher velocities to be eroded from a stream bed than medium sand does, even though they settle very slowly once suspended.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson claims only that transport capacity rises with velocity and that coarser grains settle first as flow slows; it avoids the erosion-side claim about which grain sizes are easiest to lift, leaving that nuance to the erosion topic.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was generic boilerplate with no river-specific content: 'Rivers is a foundational concept in Earth & Space Science', the 'label on a toolbox drawer' framing, and the advice to memorize definitions with context were unverified and were discarded entirely.

Added five source-backed practice questions with answer keys distributed across A/B/C/D (A:1, B:1, C:2, D:1).

Kept general erosion, groundwater, glaciers, and soil mechanics out of scope per the sibling-topic map.

sourceRecords.title: Physical Geology, 13.2 Drainage Basins
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC (Steven Earle)
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused verbatim (id and URL identical). Read via an Internet Archive capture (snapshot 2024-04-15 re-confirmed 2026-08-21). Supports: a stream as flowing surface water of any size; a drainage basin as the area from which water flows to form a stream; the boundary between two drainage basins as the height of land between them (drainage divide); gradient computed as change in elevation divided by distance; base level as the lowest level a stream can erode down to; graded streams as steepest in their headwaters with gradient gradually decreasing toward a smooth profile.

sourceRecords.title: Physical Geology, 13.3 Stream Erosion and Deposition
sourceRecords.provider: BCcampus Open Education / Open Textbook BC (Steven Earle)
sourceRecords.notes: Existing registry record reused verbatim (id and URL identical). Read via an Internet Archive capture (snapshot 2024-02-24 re-confirmed 2026-08-21; a 2026-06-09 capture was read by the sibling erosion topic's verification pass and supports the levee/floodplain deposit pattern). Supports: flowing water as a very important mechanism for both erosion and deposition; bedload moved by saltation and traction; suspended load; dissolved load averaging about 15 percent of the mass transported; faster flow keeping larger particles in suspension; deposition when velocity drops; levee deposits coarsest near the channel and progressively finer across the floodplain.
